name: Business Model & Monetization Design
description: A warm editorial strategy system for making customer value exchange, ecosystem roles, revenue architecture, pricing logic, unit economics, and validation gates visible as one coherent business model.
style_guide:
# Editorial Business Model & Monetization Design

## Design intent

Create a thoughtful business-model deck that explains how customer pain becomes delivered value, how participants and capabilities fit together, how money flows, what the economics look like, and which assumptions must be validated before scale. The visual system should feel like a premium strategy notebook: warm parchment, deep navy ink, terracotta emphasis, muted gold and sage support, elegant serif conclusions, precise mono annotations, and flat analytical exhibits.

This is not a filled-in canvas exercise or a pricing-page mockup. The deck must expose causal relationships among customer job, value exchange, ecosystem role, revenue driver, cost driver, and unit economics. Preserve the compositional character of the reference images, but never copy their customer segments, prices, revenue mix, economics, partners, milestones, or recommendations. The previews are visual examples only; this guide is the authoring authority.

## Core visual signature

- Use warm parchment as the default canvas with deep navy for structure and terracotta for the central monetization thesis.
- Pair a refined editorial serif with a neutral sans-serif and restrained mono labels.
- Use large short conclusions, diagrammatic value flows, concentric or layered business-model structures, restrained charts, and small evidence notes.
- Favor square or lightly softened panels, thin warm-gray rules, matte fills, and generous margins.
- Use muted sage for partner, capability, or validation context and gold for value transfer or economic linkage; neither should compete with terracotta.
- The cover may include one isometric system illustration. Analytical pages should rely primarily on diagrams and evidence.

## Canvas, grid, and spacing

- Author on a fixed `1280 × 720 px` 16:9 canvas.
- Keep `64–72 px` side margins, `44–52 px` top space, and `28–36 px` for footer notes.
- Use a 12-column grid with `20–24 px` gutters. Align diagrams, charts, cards, and labels to shared lines.
- Allow `140–180 px` for an eyebrow and editorial conclusion before the main exhibit on analytical pages.
- Use `24–32 px` between major modules, `14–20 px` between related elements, and `8–12 px` between labels and values.
- Prefer balanced `6/6` value-exchange structures, an `8/4` model-and-implication split, three equal revenue modules, or a full-width validation table.
- Maintain broad negative space; do not turn parchment into a crowded worksheet.

## Color system

### Primary palette

- Warm parchment: `#F4EFE6`. Use for the default canvas and quiet context zones.
- Strategy navy: `#173653`. Use for titles, diagrams, axes, key totals, and strong evidence panels.
- Terracotta: `#BE5B36`. Use for the monetization thesis, primary customer tension, recommended pricing move, and decisive assumption.
- Warm white: `#FBF9F4`. Use for exhibit cards, comparison panels, and inset evidence surfaces.
- Muted gold: `#D0A83F`. Use for value transfer, revenue linkage, pricing anchors, and selected economic bridges.
- Muted sage: `#859578`. Use for partners, capabilities, validation states, and secondary ecosystem roles.
- Body graphite: `#39434C`; hairline warm gray: `#D8CFC0`.

### Semantic exceptions

- Negative red: `#A9473D`. Use only for failed economics, kill signals, or violated guardrails.
- Positive green: `#4F8065`. Use only for validated assumptions or passed gates.
- Keep exceptions out of the template's primary color tags.

## Typography

- Use `Source Serif 4`, `Cormorant Garamond`, or a similar editorial serif for page conclusions and short thesis statements.
- Use `Inter`, `Arial`, or a neutral grotesk for explanations, diagrams, charts, and tables.
- Use `IBM Plex Mono`, `Roboto Mono`, or a similar mono face for formulas, assumptions, sources, units, test IDs, and scenario labels.
- Cover titles may be `54–68 px`; page conclusions `36–48 px`; body text `16–19 px`; labels `11–14 px`; key figures `28–42 px`.
- Italic serif may emphasize one phrase about value, willingness to pay, or scalable economics. Do not italicize whole paragraphs.

## Persistent frame

- Use a compact section label at upper-left and a page number at upper-right, separated from content by a thin navy or warm-gray rule.
- Add a short bottom takeaway, formula definition, or source strip when needed.
- Use terracotta navigation accents sparingly and maintain consistent page numbering.
- Assumption, target, observed, and validated states must use consistent labels throughout the deck.

## Page archetypes

### Cover and monetization context

Use a calm parchment cover with one editorial title, short business question, owner/date, and one restrained isometric illustration of the value system. Do not use an ornamental illustration unrelated to the operating model.

### Customer problem and value exchange

Separate ideal customer, job, pain, current alternative, desired gain, and willingness-to-pay evidence. Use a two-way exchange diagram to show what the customer gives and receives, including money, time, data, risk, service, or outcome where relevant.

### Business model and ecosystem roles

Use a concentric, layered, or structured canvas that links value proposition, customer segments, channels, relationships, activities, resources, partners, and platform roles. Arrows must describe actual flows, not decorate the model.

### Revenue streams and pricing logic

Compare recurring, usage, transaction, services, licensing, or other relevant streams. Show revenue basis, payer, trigger, unit, price logic, expected mix, and strategic role. Use a tier ladder only when tiers correspond to real differences in value, entitlement, or cost to serve.

### Cost structure and unit economics

Combine a restrained cost allocation view with a single-customer or single-unit P&L. Define gross margin, contribution margin, CAC, payback, retention, expansion, and cost-to-serve consistently. Show current, target, and modeled cases as distinct states.

### Assumptions, validation, and scale path

Rank critical assumptions by importance and uncertainty. For each, show evidence, test, owner, date, threshold, and kill or pivot signal. End with a three-horizon scale path tied to validated economics and explicit guardrails rather than calendar ambition alone.

## Data and evidence integrity

- Never invent willingness to pay, pricing, revenue mix, conversion, retention, churn, expansion, CAC, margin, market size, cost, or payback.
- Distinguish observed transaction data, customer research, benchmark evidence, management estimate, target, and modeled scenario.
- Define the payer, user, beneficiary, unit of value, billing unit, recognition basis, and period for each revenue stream.
- Show whether costs are fixed, variable, step-fixed, allocated, or excluded from contribution margin.
- Do not mix bookings, billings, recognized revenue, cash collection, GMV, and gross profit.
- State cohort, segment, geography, currency, and time basis for economic metrics.

## Imagery and iconography

- Default to diagrams, formulas, model canvases, and restrained charts.
- One cover illustration may depict an ecosystem, platform, product, or value flow in a clean isometric style using the palette.
- Use minimal line icons for customer, channel, partner, resource, payment, and experiment labels.
- Avoid coins, cash piles, pricing-page screenshots, handshake imagery, decorative gears, and generic startup illustrations.

## Content rules

- Each slide must make one model claim and expose its evidence or assumption status.
- Keep customer value, monetization mechanism, revenue recognition, and unit economics visibly distinct.
- Make trade-offs explicit: adoption versus capture, simplicity versus segmentation, growth versus margin, control versus ecosystem leverage.
- Use formulas only when inputs are defined and sourced.
- Make the next validation decision visible: continue, redesign, narrow segment, adjust pricing, or stop.

## Avoid

- Do not reuse preview company names, segments, prices, economics, partners, assumptions, illustrations, or milestones.
- Do not turn the deck into a generic Business Model Canvas with nine equally weighted boxes.
- Do not use every palette color on every page; terracotta should remain the scarce decisive accent.
- Do not imply product tiers are validated without willingness-to-pay or packaging evidence.
- Do not present a target unit-economics model as current performance.
- Do not use gradients, glass effects, heavy shadows, 3D charts, oversized radii, or decorative blobs.
- Do not repeat identical card grids; adapt the structure to value exchange, ecosystem, pricing, economics, or validation.
